strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: scaling neural amortized causal discovery to large graphs (up to 1,000 nodes) where existing neural architectures like AVICI encounter severe memory and runtime bottlenecks.

Well-motivated architectural design combining hierarchical sample-dimension reduction, tied axial attention, and a two-stream interaction mechanism (DataGraph block) that efficiently balances representation capacity and computational footprint.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse synthetic mechanisms (linear, NN, sigmoid, polynomial) and semi-synthetic single-cell gene regulatory networks (SERGIO), consistently demonstrating superior accuracy (mAP, AUC, SHD, OA, and AID metrics) alongside 4x to 13,000x speedups over baselines.

Extensive ablations and diagnostic analyses, including evaluations of reduction strategies, graph priors, prediction heads, latent confounding, prior noise sensitivity, and cycle-breaking post-processing.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to synthetic SCMs and semi-synthetic simulated datasets (SERGIO); evaluation on established real-world causal benchmark datasets (such as Sachs flow cytometry or real scRNA-seq with CRISPR knockouts) is missing to substantiate out-of-distribution real-world transfer.

The formulation relies on the inverse sample covariance matrix as a statistical graph prior, but the paper does not clarify how rank deficiency or ill-conditioning is handled when the sample size is on par with or smaller than the number of variables (e.g., high-dimensional regimes).

Acyclicity is not strictly enforced during inference, resulting in noticeable cycle emergence on out-of-distribution graph sizes and mechanisms (e.g., 100% cyclic graphs requiring up to ~103 edge removals in the polynomial n=1000 setting).

Many architectural components (tied attention from Rao et al., the pairwise edge-classification head from Wu et al., and the axial transformer backbone from Lorch et al.) are adaptations of existing techniques, meaning novelty lies mainly in systems/architecture synthesis rather than fundamentally new causal principles.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental scalability bottleneck in amortized causal discovery: while prior neural methods like AVICI struggle beyond 50-100 variables due to memory and compute overheads, CauScale successfully trains on up to 500 nodes and performs zero-shot inference on 1,000 nodes.

Well-motivated architecture combining hierarchical sample-dimension reduction, tied axial attention, and a two-stream (data stream + graph stream) message passing framework, balancing compute efficiency with structural information preservation.

Impressive empirical efficiency and performance: achieves significant speedups (4x to over 13,000x compared to existing baselines) while maintaining superior or highly competitive mAP, SHD, and AID scores across synthetic SCMs and semi-synthetic SERGIO single-cell GRN benchmarks.

Thorough experimental validation and ablation studies covering out-of-distribution graph sizes and causal mechanisms, sample size sensitivity, latent confounder robustness, attention tying, and pooling strategies.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to synthetic SCMs and semi-synthetic SERGIO simulations; testing on real-world benchmarks with known ground truth (e.g., Sachs protein-signaling dataset, or experimental perturbation benchmarks in single-cell genomics) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

The sample-dimension pooling mechanism lacks theoretical justification: while pooling sample representations along depth saves substantial computation, causal identifiability (especially for non-linear non-Gaussian models) relies heavily on higher-order joint distributional statistics that could be distorted by progressive chunk pooling.

The method does not natively enforce acyclicity: at scale (e.g., n=1000) or under out-of-distribution mechanisms, predicted graphs frequently contain cycles (up to 100% in the polynomial case), necessitating a greedy heuristic cycle-breaking post-processing step.

High sensitivity to the graph prior at large graph scales: Table 4 indicates that when prior estimation is noisy (e.g., small sample count relative to dimension), performance degrades substantially (from 64.9% down to 32.6% mAP for n=1000), and the manuscript does not discuss how matrix inversion is handled when m < n.

strengths: Substantial scalability and efficiency gains: CauScale directly addresses the memory and runtime bottlenecks that plague amortized causal discovery models (e.g., AVICI), successfully scaling training to 500-node graphs and inference to 1,000-node graphs with up to 20,000 samples where baseline methods encounter Out-Of-Memory failures.

Principled and well-motivated architecture: The combination of tied axial attention (reducing attention map memory footprint from O(R H C^2) to O(H C^2)) and progressive observation-dimension pooling (reduction unit) is well reasoned for i.i.d. data, supported by formal FLOP and peak activation memory analyses.

Comprehensive experimental suite: The paper evaluates across synthetic SCMs and semi-synthetic gene regulatory networks (SERGIO), comparing against diverse paradigms (constraint-based, score-based, continuous optimization, and amortized methods) across multiple metrics (SHD, mAP, AUC, OA, AID).

Detailed ablation studies: The ablations systematically validate each core design component, including the reduction unit, pooling strategies, graph stream, inductive graph prior, and pairwise prediction head.
weaknesses: Absence of real-world data evaluation: Experiments are strictly confined to synthetic SCMs and simulator-generated data (SERGIO). Validating on real biological data with established interventions or ground truth (e.g., perturb-seq or protein-signaling benchmarks) is missing, leaving its utility in messy real-world regimes unproven.

Handling of ill-conditioned / singular covariance matrices: The graph prior explicitly relies on the inverse covariance matrix. The paper does not specify how this inversion is stabilized when the sample size is small relative to node count (m < n) or when variables are collinear/singular.

Severe cyclicity under distribution shifts: Because acyclicity is not enforced during network prediction, cyclicity degrades noticeably on out-of-distribution mechanisms and large graphs (reaching 100% on polynomial graphs at n = 1000, requiring an average removal of 103 edges via a post-hoc heuristic).

Sensitivity to observation ordering in reduction unit: The reduction unit performs chunked average pooling over the observation dimension. For non-temporal, exchangeable i.i.d. data, grouping adjacent observations into chunks could introduce sensitivity to sample ordering or permutation, which is neither analyzed nor ablated.

strengths: Addresses an important and pressing bottleneck in amortized causal discovery: scaling transformer-based architectures to large graphs ($n \ge 500$) and large sample sizes where previous models like AVICI run out of memory.

Well-motivated architectural design that combines progressive sample-dimension reduction, tied axial attention (adapted from MSA Transformers), and a two-stream interaction mechanism that preserves structural relational signals while compressing data embeddings.

Impressive empirical scalability and inference speed, demonstrating zero-shot inference on 1,000-node graphs in under 1 second with high mAP/AUC, yielding orders-of-magnitude speedups over continuous optimization and classical search methods.

Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse graph topologies (Erdős-Rényi, Scale-Free, SBM), functional mechanisms, and realistic biological dynamics (SERGIO-GRN simulator), supported by informative ablations dissecting each component's contribution.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on dense interventional regimes: the training data assumes single-node hard interventions covering all variables (in a 1:n observational-to-interventional ratio). In many real-world large-scale applications ($n \ge 500$), intervening on every node is prohibitively expensive or infeasible; the manuscript lacks detailed analysis of performance under purely observational or sparse interventional regimes.

Potential confounding in baseline comparisons: as noted in Appendix C, AVICI could not be retrained on the authors' training setup due to out-of-memory errors and was evaluated using off-the-shelf repository checkpoints (`scm-v0` and `neurips-grn`). While this highlights AVICI's memory bottlenecks, differences in pre-training data distributions could partially confound the accuracy comparison in Table 1.

Assumptions regarding the graph prior: using the inverse empirical covariance matrix $\rho = \mathrm{Cov}(D)^{-1}$ as a prior works when the sample size $m > n$, but becomes ill-conditioned or singular in high-dimensional low-sample regimes ($m < n$). The paper does not address how the architecture handles singular sample covariances or whether regularized estimators (e.g., Graphical Lasso) should be used.

A few minor presentation lapses: an incomplete project link in the abstract ('Our project page is at .'), typos such as 'DaraGraph Block' in Figure 2 caption, and incomplete bibliographic entries (e.g., missing publication years/venues for Nazaret et al.).

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: scaling amortized (zero-shot) neural causal discovery to large graphs (up to 1,000 nodes at test time and 500 nodes during training), where existing deep methods like AVICI suffer severe memory and runtime bottlenecks.

Well-motivated architectural design that targets both time and memory complexity by combining progressive observation reduction (the Reduction Unit), tied axial attention weights across axes, and a dual-stream (data and graph) interaction scheme.

Impressive computational efficiency gains: inference takes less than a second on 1,000-node graphs, delivering orders-of-magnitude speedups compared to optimization-based methods (NOTEARS, SDCD) and partition-based amortized baselines (SEA).

Extensive experimental evaluation on both synthetic SCMs and semi-synthetic gene regulatory networks (SERGIO-GRN), accompanied by informative ablation studies examining each architectural module (tied attention, reduction unit, graph prior, and pooling strategies).
weaknesses: Mathematical imprecision in the formulation of the statistical graph prior: Section 4.1 defines the inverse covariance prior as $\rho = (\mathbb{E}[(D - \mu)(D - \mu)^\top])^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$. Given that data $D$ is defined with dimensions $m \times n$, $(D - \mu)(D - \mu)^\top$ yields an $m \times m$ matrix rather than $n \times n$. Furthermore, when $n=1000$ and sample size $m=1000$, empirical covariance is ill-conditioned or rank-deficient; the paper does not clarify how matrix inversion, regularization, or pseudo-inversion is handled in high dimensions.

Over-reliance on dense interventional data: The synthetic setup assumes interventional data covering all nodes (1:n observational to single-node intervention ratio), which significantly simplifies causal orientation and identifiability. The paper lacks evaluation on purely observational data or regimes with sparse/unknown interventions.

Unfair baseline comparison for AVICI: Appendix C mentions using off-the-shelf public checkpoints (`scm-v0`) for AVICI rather than training on the exact same data distributions as CauScale, which partly accounts for AVICI's near-zero performance on the larger synthetic test splits.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic and simulated data: While SERGIO simulates realistic SDE gene regulatory dynamics, there is no validation on real-world benchmark datasets (such as Sachs protein signaling or real perturbation screens like Perturb-seq) to demonstrate practical utility in noisy real-world settings.

Cycle analysis is limited to small graphs ($n \le 100$ in Figure 5): Because acyclicity is not explicitly constrained, it remains unclear how many directed cycles are produced when scaling to $n=500$ or $n=1000$ nodes.

strengths: Addresses a critical and practical bottleneck in amortized causal discovery: the severe memory and computational scaling issues of attention-based models when scaling to large graphs (e.g., hundreds or thousands of nodes).

The architectural design is well-motivated: combining axial attention with tied attention weights (borrowed from MSA Transformer) and periodic observation-dimension reduction effectively cuts memory and FLOP requirements while preserving structural causal information via the dual-stream data/graph design.

Empirical results are strong: CauScale achieves substantial speedups (up to orders of magnitude over classical and optimization-based methods, and several times faster than AVICI/SEA) while scaling to 1000-node graphs at test time and successfully training on 500-node graphs where prior transformer-based amortized methods ran out of memory.

Comprehensive experimental suite including synthetic graphs, out-of-distribution causal mechanisms (sigmoid, polynomial), and biological regulatory networks (SERGIO-GRN), supported by clear ablation studies examining each component (tied attention, reduction unit, pooling methods, and prediction heads).
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is primarily architectural integration and engineering: the individual components (tied axial attention from Rao et al. (2021), amortized causal learning framework from Lorch et al. (2022), and decomposed edge prediction heads from Lippe et al. (2021)) are existing techniques adapted together rather than fundamentally new causal discovery theory.

In Section 4.1, the mathematical definition of the inverse covariance prior contains a dimensional/notational inconsistency: with data matrix $D \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, the covariance over variables should be formulated as $(D-\mu)^\top(D-\mu) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, rather than $(D-\mu)(D-\mu)^\top$. Furthermore, details regarding how the inverse is computed when $m \approx n$ or in ill-conditioned cases (e.g., pseudo-inverse, ridge regularization) should be explicitly clarified.

Comparison fairness regarding AVICI: As noted in Appendix C, CauScale was trained directly on the newly generated synthetic and SERGIO training distributions, whereas AVICI was evaluated using off-the-shelf repository checkpoints (`scm-v0`, `neurips-grn`) because retraining AVICI encountered OOM. While this underscores AVICI's memory bottleneck, evaluating an off-the-shelf checkpoint on a potentially shifted data distribution could confound the accuracy comparison.

Acyclicity is not guaranteed: Although the decomposed prediction head empirically produces low cyclicity on small graphs (Figure 5), the paper does not report cyclicity metrics (e.g., number of cycles or percentage of DAG predictions) for large-scale graphs ($n=500$ or $n=1000$), where cycle accumulation is typically more severe.
Minor presentation issues, such as the incomplete project link at the end of the abstract on page 1 ('Our project page is at .').
